Every archive answers differently, so the chasing had to be automated

A request to a Polish state archive is not an API call. It is a letter, or a form, or an e-mail to
an address that changes, and the reply comes when it comes.

The old way was a spreadsheet and somebody's memory. The failure was never a lost document — it
was a request that quietly aged four months because nobody was reminded.

A queue where each request knows which archive it went to, what that archive's usual answer time
is, and when it should be chased. It does not send anything on its own. It puts three items on a
person's desk each morning, in the order that matters.
Average wait did not change — archives are archives.

went from eleven to zero.
Eleven archives, eleven habits. Some answer in a week, some in four months, one only to letters. The fix was a queue with memory, not a faster clerk.

One program became six services and intake stopped breaking on Mondays

The office ran on one program that did everything: intake, scanning, text recognition, filing,
mail. It worked for two years and failed in a specific, predictable way — Monday scanning would
saturate the machine and nobody could open a case file.

Splitting it had nothing to do with scale. Six small services meant the slow one could be slow on
its own, be restarted alone, and be replaced without anyone noticing.
The part I would warn anyone about:
six services means six ways to be half-deployed.

The
first month cost more in confusion than the old crashes cost in time. It paid back in the second.
The intake system fell over whenever scanning ran. Splitting it was not about scale — it was about one slow job no longer taking the office down.
Why client documents never leave the building
The commercial services are better than what I run. That was never the question.

The question is what happens to a scan of somebody's grandmother's birth certificate after it has
been useful — where it is stored, who may look at it, and which country's law applies. For a legal
practice those answers have to be short, and "on a machine in this room" is the shortest one.

The cost is real and I will not pretend otherwise: worse recognition on the hardest pages, a card
that has to be bought and cooled, and evenings spent on things a subscription would have solved.
A birth certificate is somebody's family. Sending it to a service that logs prompts was never going to be acceptable, so the models had to come here instead.
Matching a name across a century of spelling

Records were written by clerks who spelled by ear, in whichever language the border currently
spoke. A family line breaks not because a document is missing but because nobody was willing to
say that two spellings are one man.

Plain string comparison is useless here. What works is a small set of rules built from what
actually happens in these records — transliteration between alphabets, endings that change with
grammar, and the handful of substitutions clerks made constantly — plus a threshold below which
a human decides and the machine does not guess.
The same person is Grzegorz, Grzegorż, Gregor and Gregory across four documents. Deciding when two names are one person is the whole job.

No archive gets an automatic message. The point was never to send more letters — it was to stop
requests ageing unnoticed.
The chasing queue. Knows each archive's habits and puts three things on a desk each morning.

Fourteen hours per case spent chasing. That single number is the reason the queue exists, and the
reason I stopped building the clever thing I had planned instead.
I measured every case for a year. The expensive part is not the law — it is waiting, and the chasing that waiting creates.
On buying software for an office that does something unusual

Every product for law firms is built for the average law firm: a client, a matter, an hourly rate,
a court date. Citizenship by descent has none of that shape. There is a dead ancestor, eleven
archives, a queue measured in months, and documents in three alphabets.

So the software is bought, and then bent. And bending it costs more than the licence, every year,
forever — except the bend is invisible, so it never appears in any budget.

I am not arguing that everyone should write their own. Most offices should not: the average firm
really is average, and the product really does fit. I am arguing that

"we are unusual" is a
measurable claim

, and if it is true, buying is the expensive option pretending to be the cheap
one.
An opinion, not a recipe. Bought software fits the average firm, and a firm doing something specific is never the average one.
